lesson.title: Checking By Hand: Manual Testing and Where It Breaks Down
lesson.summary: Manual testing means running a program with chosen inputs and checking the output by eye, which is the natural starting point for testing but becomes slow and unreliable as a program grows.
lesson.body:
The simplest form testing can take is also the most familiar one: write some code, run it, look at what it prints, and decide for yourself whether that output looks right. That is manual testing, and it is exactly what square(4) == 16 demonstrated in the last lesson, a person reading the printed True and confirming, by their own judgment, that the function behaved correctly on that particular input.

```python
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0

print(is_even(4))
print(is_even(7))
print(is_even(-2))
print(is_even(0))
```

is_even(4) computes 4 % 2, which is 0, and 0 == 0 is True. is_even(7) computes 7 % 2, which is 1, and 1 == 0 is False. is_even(-2) computes -2 % 2, and in Python the % operator always returns a result with the same sign as the divisor, so -2 % 2 is 0, and 0 == 0 is True. is_even(0) computes 0 % 2, which is 0, and 0 == 0 is True. Output:

```
True
False
True
True
```

A person running this has to know, before looking, that they expected True, False, True, True, then compare that expectation against what actually printed. That comparison step lives entirely in the tester's head, or at best in a comment above the code.

Manual testing this way is genuinely useful, especially while first writing a function or exploring how it behaves, and it costs nothing to set up, no special tools, just print(). But it has real limits. Every time is_even() changes, even slightly, someone has to rerun this same script and re-check all four lines by eye again, and it is easy to get complacent and skip a case, or misread a True as a False while scanning quickly. The check also leaves no lasting record: there is nothing that proves these four specific cases were ever verified, beyond someone's memory of having looked at the output once.

None of that makes manual testing wrong, it is often the fastest way to get a first read on whether a new function is roughly working. But it does not scale to a program with dozens of functions that all need to keep working correctly as the code keeps changing, and it depends entirely on a human doing the comparing, which is exactly the part that can be automated instead. That automation is what unit testing, covered next, is built around.
